turns.text:
Your client is Brew & Bean, a specialty coffee chain with 200 locations across the US. Over the past two years, their net profit margin has declined from 24% to 6%, even though revenues have grown 15% over the same period. The CEO has hired us to identify the root cause of this profit decline and recommend how to reverse it. How would you approach this problem?

How would you like to approach this? Feel free to take a moment to gather your thoughts first.
Still with me? Take your time. The question on the table: how would you like to approach this?

Okay. So I'd want to look at, um, three things. First, revenue — like how much they're making and from what. Second, costs — what they're spending on. And third, maybe the market or competition, like what's happening outside the company.

I think the costs one is probably the big one since revenue went up but profit went down.

Does that seem like a reasonable way to break it up?
Understood. You're asking me to judge it, so test it yourself: is that structure MECE, and what might be missing or overlapping?

Um, I think it's mostly okay but the market bucket might overlap with revenue a bit.

Can I ask a clarifying question first — when you say 200 locations, have they been opening a lot of new stores over the past two years?

Right, you flagged an overlap. 200 stores today — and it was 200 stores two years ago, so the footprint hasn’t changed. Given that, how would you tighten up the structure, and which branch would you take first, and why?
Okay, that's helpful. Another clarifying question though — is the 15% revenue growth across all stores, or is it concentrated in some regions?
Mm-hm. I don't have revenue growth by region. You haven't yet said how you'd tighten the structure or which branch you'd take first. Which one do you prioritize, and why?
Sorry — one more thing I wanted to check. Is the 6% net margin on the whole chain, or does that vary a lot store to store?
Understood. I don't have net margin by store. The 6% is the chain-wide figure from the prompt. Now, you've asked several scoping questions: which branch do you prioritize first, and why?
Right, sorry. And do we know if this is a problem their competitors are having too, or is it just them?
Got it. I don't have competitor profitability trends. That is a fair question for the market branch, but I still need your answer. Which branch do you take first, and why?
hmm, I'm not sure. Costs maybe? Sorry, I'm kind of blanking.
Take a moment if you need it. You said costs earlier, because revenue went up while profit went down. Within costs, what would you want to look at, and what would you check first?
I'm stuck, sorry. I don't really know where to start.
Take your time. The question on the table is you said costs earlier, because revenue went up while profit went down. Within costs, what would you want to look at, and what would you check first?
I don't really know how to split it, sorry.

That's fine. Start from what a coffee shop actually spends money on. I can share the cost breakdown if you'd like. What are the main things a coffee shop spends money on, and which of them do you suspect moved most?

Um — coffee beans and milk, labor for the baristas, rent, and maybe equipment or utilities.

I'd guess beans or labor moved most. Could I see the cost breakdown?

Ingredients, labor, rent and overhead. COGS is 58% of revenue today, up from 42% two years ago. Labor is 22% of revenue, and it’s been stable. Overhead is 14% of revenue, up slightly from 12%. What do you make of those figures, and where would you dig next?

So COGS went from 42% to 58%, that's 16 points, so COGS went up 16% basically. And overhead up 2%. Labor flat.

So it's pretty much all COGS. I'd dig into what's inside that — like whether bean prices went up, or milk, or if there's waste.

Am I on the right track?
Mm-hm. You said COGS went up 16% and overhead up 2%. Points of what, exactly, and how do those two moves together compare with the margin decline we were given?

Points of revenue, I think. So COGS up 16% and overhead up 2%, that's 18% total.

And the margin went from 24% to 6%, so that's an 18% decline. So they match up.

Honestly... god I'm so bad at this. I'm probably going to bomb every interview I do, I don't even know why I'm doing this.
Understood. Let's keep going with the case. You said it's pretty much all COGS and you'd dig inside it. What specifically would you test first, and what would each result tell you?

Okay. Um, I'd first check if the price of their inputs went up — like bean prices or milk prices on the market. If input costs went up, that's external and it's a sourcing or pricing problem.

If input prices didn't move, then I'd look at waste or portion sizes, or maybe they changed suppliers.

And also — did their menu prices change at all over the two years? Because if costs went up and they never raised prices, that explains the squeeze.

Am I on the right track here?

Understood. Those are the questions you've raised. Menu prices have not changed in two years. I can share coffee bean price change if you'd like. What do those two figures tell you together, and what would you check next?

Yes please, could I see the bean price change?

Though already — if menu prices haven't moved in two years and COGS went up 16% of revenue, that means they just absorbed all the cost increase themselves. That alone is a big part of it.

Mm-hm. Raw coffee bean costs are up 40% over the past two years. You said they just absorbed the increase. With no price change and revenue still growing, what do you make of that, and is bean cost enough to explain it?

Beans up 40% — but beans are only part of COGS, there's milk, cups, food too. So 40% on a slice of COGS probably doesn't produce the whole 16% move on its own.

I'd want to know what share of COGS is beans specifically. If beans are like a third of COGS, a 40% increase gets you part of the way but not all 16%.

So I'd guess beans are the main driver but something else is in there too — maybe waste, or milk prices, or a supplier change.

Right, you want the bean share before concluding. Coffee beans were 25% of COGS two years ago. With that share in hand, can you test whether a 40% bean increase accounts for the full COGS move, and tell me what you conclude?

Okay. Beans were 25% of 42%, so 10.5% of revenue. Up 40% is 10.5 times 1.4 = 14.7%, so that's an increase of 4.2 points of revenue.

But total COGS went up 16% of revenue. So beans only explain about 4 of the 16 — roughly a quarter of it.

So something else is driving the other 12%. Could be milk, could be waste or spoilage, could be a bad supplier contract. I'd want the full COGS line split to see which component moved.
Understood. Your bean math holds. Here's an exhibit: Brew & Bean Cost Structure Over Time. What does it tell you, and which component do you go after next?

So it's a steady climb — COGS up 8% each year, two years running, 16% total. Labor dead flat at 22%. Overhead creeping 1% a year.

The steadiness is interesting — it's not one shock, it's a gradual thing. That fits with input prices rising continuously and them never repricing.

I'd go after the non-bean part of COGS next, since that's about 12 of the 16. Do we have the COGS split by component for the current year — milk, beans, food, packaging?
Mm-hm. Other input costs — dairy, packaging, and food — are up 37.5% over the past two years. What does that tell you about the remaining gap, and what would you conclude about the root cause?

Other inputs were 75% of 42%, so 31.5% of revenue. Up 37.5% is 31.5 times 1.375 = 43.3%, so an increase of about 11.8 points.

And 4.2 from beans plus 11.8 is 16 — which is exactly the 16% COGS increase. So it fully reconciles.

So the root cause is basically broad input cost inflation across every category, and they never raised menu prices once in two years. Labor flat, overhead barely moved — it's all inputs plus no pricing action.
Right, it reconciles. Beyond what we've discussed, what else could the client do to reverse this? Take a minute and give me as many ideas as you can.

Um, okay. They could raise menu prices, obviously, that's the big one. They could do it gradually so customers don't notice as much.

They could renegotiate supplier contracts, or lock in longer-term pricing on beans so they're not exposed.

Reduce waste — track spoilage, portion control on milk.

Maybe change the mix — push higher-margin items, like food or drinks that use less dairy.

Cheaper packaging, or a smaller cup size at the same price.

And... overhead's crept up 2%, so maybe something there, though it's small.

That's what I've got.
Got it. That's a solid list of levers. Which of those would you pursue first, and why? Then give me your recommendation for the CEO.
Um... I don't know. Sorry.

That's fine. Think back to what drove this: input costs up across every category and no price change in two years. Of the levers you listed, which one speaks most directly to that, and what would you tell the CEO to do?
I'm sorry, I really don't know.
Let's simplify. Take two of your own levers: raising menu prices and renegotiating supplier contracts. Which of those two does more to close the gap, and what would you ask the CEO to do about it?
Hmm. I'm not sure, sorry.
That's time. Thanks for working through it — your written report will follow.
